scenes.tts: Flat on his back with a sinus infection at Oxford in March 1948, Pauling asked his wife to bring him paper and a slide rule, drew a polypeptide chain on an ordinary sheet, and folded it into a right-handed coil that came around every 3.6 residues — the alpha helix.
scenes.narration: Flat on his back with a sinus infection at Oxford in March 1948, Pauling asked his wife to bring him paper and a slide rule, drew a polypeptide chain on an ordinary sheet, and folded it into a right-handed coil that came around every 3.6 residues — the alpha helix.

scenes.tts: He had cracked it by throwing out the assumption everyone else clung to: that the coil had to close after a whole number of amino acids.

scenes.tts: The following year, working with Harvey Itano, he ran sickle-cell and healthy hemoglobin through electrophoresis and watched them drift at different speeds — the first time anyone pinned a specific human illness to a specific defect in a specific molecule.
scenes.narration: The following year, working with Harvey Itano, he ran sickle-cell and healthy hemoglobin through electrophoresis and watched them drift at different speeds — the first time anyone pinned a specific human illness to a specific defect in a specific molecule.

scenes.tts: He called it a "molecular disease," and the phrase reframed medicine: a single changed amino acid could be the whole catastrophe. Vernon Ingram would later locate the exact lesion — one glutamate swapped for a valine at the sixth position of the beta chain — but the conceptual leap was Pauling's.

scenes.tts: He holds two unshared Nobel Prizes, Chemistry and Peace, and proposed a triple helix for DNA that was wrong in nearly every particular, partly because the government had pulled his passport and he never saw the photographs at King's College.
